title: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
subject: Medicine
summary: A median‑nerve entrapment at the wrist causing nocturnal paresthesia, sensory loss in the thumb, index and middle fingers, and possible motor weakness. Diagnosis is clinical, confirmed by nerve conduction if available.

sections.p: Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) is compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel, producing sensory and motor symptoms. In low‑resource settings, diagnosis relies on history and bedside tests; nerve conduction studies confirm severity when available.
b: Nocturnal tingling in thumb, index, middle fingers

t.b: Does tapping over the carpal tunnel elicit tingling? Positive suggests median nerve irritation.
Does sustained wrist flexion reproduce symptoms? Positive supports CTS.
Measures median nerve latency and amplitude. Prolonged distal latency (>3.5 ms) or reduced amplitude confirms compression.
Assesses motor unit activity in abductor pollicis brevis; abnormal findings support severe CTS.

sections.p: Severity is staged by symptom duration, motor involvement, and electrophysiology. The Boston Carpal Tunnel Questionnaire (BCCTQ) is useful when available.
b: Stage I – sensory only, mild symptoms
Stage II – sensory + mild motor weakness
Stage III – marked motor loss, atrophy

sections.p: In East Africa, the most common causes are diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, and pregnancy. Other tropical factors include parasitic infections (schistosomiasis), herbal remedies causing edema, and HIV‑related neuropathy.
b: Diabetes mellitus – chronic hyperglycaemia damages nerves

sections.p: Patients report burning or tingling that awakens them at night, worsens with wrist flexion, and may progress to weakness of thumb opposition.
When resources allow, NCS/EMG confirm diagnosis. In their absence, a thorough history and Tinel/Phalen tests suffice.

t.b: Prolonged latency or reduced amplitude confirms CTS; absence of findings suggests alternative diagnoses.

sections.p: Urgent referral is needed if there is rapid motor loss, loss of sensation in the median nerve distribution, or signs of systemic infection.

Treat underlying cause first. Supportive care includes night splints and ergonomic advice. Pharmacotherapy with NSAIDs or corticosteroids is considered when inflammation is prominent. Surgery is reserved for refractory cases.
b: Night wrist splint – reduces nocturnal pressure

t.b: Reduces median nerve swelling; avoid in diabetic patients with poor wound healing.
Indicated when conservative measures fail or motor function deteriorates; avoids long‑term disability.

sections.p: Re‑evaluate symptom progression every 3–6 months. Prevent recurrence by controlling diabetes, avoiding repetitive wrist strain, and maintaining healthy weight.
Cubital tunnel syndrome, cervical radiculopathy, and peripheral neuropathies can mimic CTS.
b: Cervical radiculopathy – neck pain radiating to arm

sections.p: Normal NCS does not exclude mild CTS; early disease may show normal electrophysiology. A negative Tinel sign does not rule out CTS.
b: Early CTS may have normal NCS
Negative Tinel can occur in mild cases

whenToSeekHelp: Fever or swelling of the wrist

faq.q: Can pregnancy cause carpal tunnel syndrome?
faq.a: Yes, fluid retention during pregnancy increases pressure in the carpal tunnel.

faq.q: Is diabetes a risk factor for CTS?
faq.a: Diabetes causes nerve damage and swelling, making CTS more likely.

faq.q: What is the best first‑line treatment in a low‑resource setting?
faq.a: Night wrist splint and ergonomic advice; NSAIDs if inflammation is suspected.

exam: What bedside test would you perform first to confirm median nerve involvement? — Tinel sign; it reproduces tingling when tapping the tunnel.
Which systemic disease is most commonly associated with CTS in East Africa? — Diabetes mellitus; it causes neuropathy and edema.
Why might a normal nerve conduction study not rule out CTS? — Early or mild CTS can have normal electrophysiology.
When is surgical release indicated? — Persistent symptoms despite splinting and medication, or progressive motor weakness.
How does pregnancy physiologically contribute to CTS? — Fluid retention increases carpal tunnel pressure.
What is the most common red flag that requires urgent referral? — Rapid loss of thumb abduction or sensory loss.
Why are corticosteroid injections avoided in poorly controlled diabetics? — They impair wound healing and increase infection risk.
What ergonomic advice would you give a patient with repetitive wrist strain? — Use wrist‑neutral positions, take frequent breaks, and use padded supports.
